chunks: From him, from Abū Yaḥyā al-Wāsiṭī, from some of his companions, from Abū al-Ḥasan al-Hāshimī, who said:

He was asked about men standing by the pool in the bathhouse: I do not distinguish the Jew from the Christian, nor the one in janabah from the one who is not in janabah. He said: “You may perform ghusl from it, and do not perform ghusl from other water, for it is purifying.”
And about a man who enters the bathhouse while he is in janabah, then touches the water without having washed it, he said: “There is no بأس in it.”
And he said: I enter the bathhouse and perform ghusl, then after the ghusl a person in janabah or not in janabah comes into contact with my body. He said: “There is no بأس in it.”

key_terms.الْجُنُبَ: a person in a state requiring ghusl due to janabah
key_terms.الْحَوْضِ: the pool or basin of water in the bathhouse
key_terms.تَغْتَسِلُ: you perform ghusl using the water
key_terms.طَهُورٌ: ritually purifying and suitable for purification
key_terms.لَا بَأْسَ: there is no harm or legal problem in it

ai.seo_question: Is bathhouse water still tahir if people of unknown status, including a junub person, use it?
ai.summary: This hadith gives legal rulings concerning shared bathhouse water and contact with others in the ḥammām. It indicates that the water of the bathhouse pool remains tahir and suitable for ghusl, and that mere contact by a junub person or bodily contact after ghusl does not, by itself, make it problematic.
